question: Six rectangles each with a common base width of \(2\) have lengths of \(1,\) \(4,\) \(9,\) \(16,\) \(25,\) and \(36.\) What is the sum of the areas of the six rectangles?
solution:
A rectangle's area is its length times its width. Since every rectangle has width \(2\), we can add the lengths first and then multiply by \(2\):
\[
2(1+4+9+16+25+36)=2\times91=182.
\]
The sum of the areas is \(182\) square units, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

edges.reason: Written addition prepares vertical alignment and repeated carrying. In multiplication the carried amount is added to one digit product, so the full three-digit column-addition procedure is not executed.

The general digit-by-digit multiplication algorithm contains digit products with seven, eight and nine. Their values are required, without demanding rote recitation as the exclusive way to obtain them.
The target explicitly distinguishes boundary length from area. Perimeter meaning is required for that contrast, not all rectangle/square perimeter computations.
Two-digit columns support larger numerical areas. Repeated unit-square counts or decomposed multiplication can also compute an area, so no fixed dimension range is imposed by this preparation link.
edges.scope: computing areas with two-digit side lengths

edges.reason: The tiled-region interpretation explains what length times width counts. The Geometric Measurement Progression develops that interpretation before treating multiplication as a formula; knowing the formula alone does not certify the tiling procedure.
edges.scope: Understanding rectangle and square area formulas as counts of square units

edges.reason: The rectangle/square area formulas count equal square units, so the meaning of area and its uniform unit are part of the asserted result.
edges.scope: interpreting length times width as unit-square count

edges.reason: Factor-order manipulation and comparison of laws help notation. An array split directly establishes distribution without the three-factor regrouping procedure.
edges.scope: rewriting forms of the distributive law
